member.name: RefinedConfidence
member.para: What the window figure was really measuring. Investigated 2026-08-28, prompted by the user asking whether later readings ever raise a mark's confidence. They never did: the value was fixed at the first accepted match and carried unchanged for ever, while the refinement's own probes - typically six per mark, up to eighteen - read the same announcement again and again and were thrown away. Measured over 32,320 announcement segments in the 159-book Perry Rhodan Silber-Edition logs, the recorded figure rises steadily with segment length: median p 0.68 at 12 characters or fewer, 0.72 at 20-40, 0.80 at 40-80, 0.97 above 160. So it partly measures how much narration Whisper packed into the segment, not how sure it is of the announcement. Worse, the window's announcement segment is routinely the one that swallowed the jingle - 8-12 s of duration holding three words, median p 0.62 - which makes the recorded value the worst-framed reading of the announcement the run ever takes.

The false-alarm rates that chose the median. The reference corpus is the only labelled data that exists here: 508 chapter marks whose positions the user confirmed by ear, so every one is known-correct and every flag raised on them is a false alarm. Measured over the frozen baseline logs:

recorded confidence (before this change) flagged 13 of 508 (2.6%); median of readings 6 (1.2%); 75th percentile 2 (0.4%); min(recorded, median) 18 (3.5%); minimum of readings 51 (10.0%). Ten of the thirteen the old rule flagged are "Corsa nello spazio", the Italian bare-number book, where the announcement is a number spoken alone and so the shortest segment there is - the flag was largely reporting announcement style. Examples of what the refinement said about marks the old rule flagged: chapter 64 recorded 0.40 against readings of 0.89-1.00 across ten probes, chapter 32 recorded 0.45 against 0.45-1.00, chapter 8 recorded 0.47 against 0.44-0.99.

The median was the user's call over the quieter 75th percentile, on the ground that the false-alarm rate can only ever argue for flagging less - on a corpus where every mark is correct, "flag nothing" scores perfectly - so it cannot by itself justify the more optimistic of two rules. There is no known-wrong population anywhere to weigh against it: across the whole 159-book library the number machinery corrected or questioned exactly one mark in 4,388, and the reference corpus was curated to correctness by construction.

Why not the best reading. Taking the maximum raises 80.6% of marks by a median of +0.140 and would make a mark look more certain the more probes the search needed. The 75th percentile raises 71.8% by +0.100, the median 57.4% by +0.045.

Rejected: the spread as a flag. The readings of one announcement - same audio, same model, window starts 0.1 s apart - disagree by a median of 0.150, p90 0.350, max 0.470, which is roughly the distance from a typical mark to the 0.5 threshold. That looked like the better signal until it was measured against the ear-verified corpus: a "spread >= 0.30" rule flags 143 of 507 (28.2%) marks known to be correct. Wide disagreement between framings is simply normal. Do not re-propose it.

Rejected: an inverse-length weighted mean (weighting each reading by 1/characters, to prefer the purest look at the announcement). It lands within 0.001 of the plain median (+0.046 against +0.045, 56.4% raised against 57.4%): the refinement probes are 4-9 s windows aimed at the announcement, so their segments are nearly all short and there is almost nothing for the weighting to separate. The sophistication buys nothing measurable.

The knock-on nobody should be surprised by. RegionProber.SkipSettledWindows reads the same figure: a low-confidence mark deliberately refuses to settle the windows it overlaps, so they keep their chance to re-detect. Raising confidences therefore makes a run skip slightly more and re-check slightly less. That is the intended consequence of the figure becoming honest, not a side effect to compensate for.
